# Incident Report — MTA 2026-01-31 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Evidence Reviewed
- `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 26.4 MB, single host capture) — only artifact present in the evidence directory. No separate Suricata/IDS export was provided.

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.1.21.58** | DHCP, NBNS, all traffic |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** (Intel NIC) | DHCP Discover/Request frames 1–3, ARP |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | DHCP option 12, NBNS registrations |
| AD domain | WIN11OFFICE.COM (NetBIOS `WIN11OFFICE`, DC `WIN-LU4L24X3UB7` at 10.1.21.2) | NBNS, LDAP/Kerberos/DNS SRV queries |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ `CNameString` between 10.1.21.58 ↔ 10.1.21.2 |

## 2. Malware Family

**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed.** No executable, hash, or YARA-matchable payload was recoverable in the clear — the actual payload transfer (~16 MB) rode entirely inside TLS to `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` (104.21.46.67), so no file hash could be extracted from this capture.

The traffic pattern is consistent with a **commodity information-stealer/loader delivered via a fake-download / anti-bot ("TDS") gate**, commonly seen in Lumma/Vidar/Stealc-class distribution chains:

1. **t=45.1s** — victim issues a `www.google.com` query (search-driven traffic).
2. **t=45.3s** — redirected to `hiyter.com` (104.21.22.231 / 172.67.207.145).
3. **t=45.8s** — redirected to `media.megafilehub4.lat` (104.21.48.156 / 172.67.154.67), a fake file-hosting/CDN domain.
4. **t=48.3–70.7s** — connection to `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` (104.21.46.67), a **16 MB TLS transfer over 22 seconds** — almost certainly the payload archive/installer download. Content unrecoverable (TLS).
5. **t=90.3s** — `whooptm.cyou` (62.72.32.156) contacted.
6. **t=92.3–103.0s** — `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49) contacted over **both port 80 (cleartext) and 443**. The cleartext HTTP exchange shows a browser check-in / anti-bot "gate" protocol: the host `GET`s `/api/set_agent?...&agent=Chrome`, receives a fingerprinting script, then `POST`s the collected fingerprint (canvas, WebGL, audio, fonts, hardware concurrency, screen res, timezone) back to `/api/set_agent?...&act=log`. This repeats for both Chrome and Edge, indicating the malware/dropper enumerates and fingerprints each installed browser individually before further activity — classic stealer/loader anti-sandbox and per-browser targeting behavior.
7. **t=122.8s and t=126.5s** — further outbound contact to `holiday-forever.cc` (80.97.160.24) and `communicationfirewall-security.cc` (104.21.9.36/172.67.141.109), consistent with continued C2 beaconing/exfil after the fingerprint gate.

No known-family string, panel name, or unique YARA-able artifact was observed, so I am **not** naming a specific malware family (e.g. "Lumma Stealer") with confidence — the evidence only supports classifying this as a **stealer/loader with a browser-fingerprinting C2 check-in gate**, distributed through a fake-download redirect chain.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

### C2 / distribution infrastructure (IP:port)
| Domain | Resolved IP(s) | Port | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| hiyter.com | 104.21.22.231, 172.67.207.145 | 443 | Redirect/gate hop |
| media.megafilehub4.lat | 104.21.48.156, 172.67.154.67 | 443 | Fake file-hosting redirect |
| arch.filemegahab4.sbs | 104.21.46.67, 172.67.136.13 | 443 | **Payload delivery** (16 MB TLS transfer) |
| whooptm.cyou | 62.72.32.156 | 443 | C2 contact |
| **whitepepper.su** | **153.92.1.49** | **80 (cleartext), 443** | **C2 check-in / browser fingerprint gate** |
| holiday-forever.cc | 80.97.160.24 | 443 | C2 contact |
| communicationfirewall-security.cc | 104.21.9.36, 172.67.141.109 | 443 | C2 contact |

### Malicious/suspicious domains
- hiyter.com
- media.megafilehub4.lat
- arch.filemegahab4.sbs
- whooptm.cyou
- whitepepper.su
- holiday-forever.cc
- communicationfirewall-security.cc

### Malicious URLs (observed in cleartext HTTP)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST, browser fingerprint exfil)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log` (POST)
- `http://whitepepper.su/favicon.ico`

Bot/gate ID and token observed: `id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`, `token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`.

### Transferred file names / hashes
- **No SHA256 hash could be extracted** — the ~16 MB payload transfer to `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` was fully TLS-encrypted; no plaintext HTTP object was exported for it.
- One templated filename string was observed inside a cleartext `whitepepper.su` HTTP response body (an embedded "cant open archive" error message, not a confirmed file transfer):
  `172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip`
  This appears to be a server-side templated string keyed to the visitor's apparent public IP rather than a hash of an actual observed binary, and should be treated as a low-confidence artifact, not a validated IOC hash.

## Summary
Host **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML (10.1.21.58, MAC 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2)**, logged in as domain user **gwyatt** on **WIN11OFFICE.COM**, browsed from a Google search result through a redirect chain (`hiyter.com` → `media.megafilehub4.lat` → `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`) that delivered a 16 MB payload over TLS, followed roughly 40 seconds later by a browser-fingerprinting check-in to `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49) for both installed browsers (Chrome and Edge), and further outbound contact to `whooptm.cyou`, `holiday-forever.cc`, and `communicationfirewall-security.cc`. This is behaviorally consistent with a commodity stealer/loader infection via a fake-download redirect chain; no signature-level (hash/YARA) confirmation is possible from this capture alone since the payload itself was never observed in plaintext.
